---
title: "Types for elements"
---

Every project so far began with a line you copied without asking what it says:

```ts
const helloWorldHeader = document.getElementById('helloWorldHeader') as HTMLHeadingElement;
```

The `as HTMLHeadingElement` at the end came with a promise that the chapter on
types for elements would explain it. This is that chapter. At the end of it
that line is gone, replaced by the one this book uses for the rest of the year.

## Ask for an element that is not there {#sec-types-for-elements-missing}

Open one of your projects from the last chapters, or create a fresh app from
the starter. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this. Note that the `as`
is gone, and that no element on the page has the id `doesNotExist`:

```ts
const header = document.getElementById('doesNotExist');

header.textContent = 'Hello';
```

Hover the mouse pointer over `header` in VS Code. The tooltip says:

```
const header: HTMLElement | null
```

The second line carries a red squiggle. Run the build in the terminal to read
the message in full:

```bash
npm run build
```

```
src/index.ts(3,1): error TS18047: 'header' is possibly 'null'.
```

TypeScript refuses to compile this, because it has no way of knowing which ids
exist on your page. So it assumes the worst.

## What the `as` was hiding {#sec-types-for-elements-cast}

Now put the cast back, exactly the way the starter had it:

```ts
const header = document.getElementById('doesNotExist') as HTMLHeadingElement;

header.textContent = 'Hello';
```

The squiggle is gone and `npm run build` is happy. Start the app with
`npm start` and open the page. Press F12 to open the browser's developer tools
and look at the console tab:

```
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'textContent')
```

Firefox words it differently, but it is the same crash. The element still does 
not exist. `as` is a sentence you say to the compiler, and the compiler 
believes you. The browser never hears it. Nothing about `as` is checked 
while your program runs, which is why the error moved from your editor, 
where you could see it, into the console, where your user meets it.

This is the kind of red line the console is for. A blank page, a heading that
keeps its old text, a click that does nothing: from now on, every one of them
starts with F12, and most of them end there too.

## Two things at once: `HTMLElement | null` {#sec-types-for-elements-union}

The type in the tooltip has a `|` in the middle, and that vertical bar means
"one of these two". A value of type `HTMLElement | null` is either an element
object or `null`, the value that stands for "nothing here". `getElementById`
returns that type because a search can fail, and TypeScript makes you deal with
both outcomes before you touch the result.

Dealing with it takes one `if`:

```ts
const header = document.getElementById('mainHeader');
if (header === null) {
  throw new Error('Element #mainHeader not found');
}

header.textContent = 'Hello';
```

`throw` stops your program right there and prints the message in the console.
That is the honest answer to a missing element: the page is not what the code
expects, so stop early with a message that names the id instead of crashing ten
lines later with a message that names nothing. Throwing errors on purpose, and
catching them, gets a chapter of its own in Part 4.

Look at the last line. After the `if`, TypeScript knows that `header` cannot be
`null` any more, so the squiggle disappears without a cast. The check also runs
in the browser, which is the whole difference from `as`: a missing element now
stops your program at the `throw`, with a message you wrote.

Most programmers write that check shorter, as `if (!header)`, because `!null`
is `true` and `!` on an element object is `false`. Both spellings mean the
same, and the chapters after this one use the short form.

## Which kind of element? {#sec-types-for-elements-kinds}

`getElementById` promises an `HTMLElement`, and that is the general kind of
element. It has what every element has, including `textContent`. Ask an
`HTMLElement` for the text a user typed and you get a second error:

```ts
const leftInput = document.getElementById('leftNumber');
if (leftInput === null) {
  throw new Error('Element #leftNumber not found');
}

console.log(leftInput.value);
```

```
src/index.ts(6,23): error TS2339: Property 'value' does not exist on type 'HTMLElement'.
```

TypeScript is right again. Only some elements have a `value`. The browser has a
more special kind for each of them: `HTMLInputElement` for `<input>` with its
`value`, `HTMLSelectElement` for `<select>`, `HTMLButtonElement` for `<button>`
with its `disabled`. Each of these is an `HTMLElement` plus its own extra
properties, so everything you can do with a general element works on an input
too. Building special kinds on top of general ones is called **inheritance**,
and in Part 4 you write your own. For now, one sentence is enough: an
`HTMLInputElement` is an `HTMLElement` that can do more.

## The course way {#sec-types-for-elements-course-way}

`document.querySelector` finds one element too, and it lets you say which kind
you expect:

```ts
const leftInput = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#leftNumber');
if (leftInput === null) {
  throw new Error('Element #leftNumber not found');
}

leftInput.value = '42';
```

Two things are new in that first line. The text in quotes is a CSS selector, so
the `#` is part of it and means "the element whose id is this"; the chapter on
selectors goes much further with that idea. The name in the angle brackets,
`<HTMLInputElement>`, tells `querySelector` which kind of element you are
asking for. Hover over `leftInput` and the tooltip says
`HTMLInputElement | null`: the kind you asked for, and still an honest `null`
for the case where nothing matches. Angle brackets like these come back in
Part 6 under the name generics. Until then, read them as "which kind I expect".

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule from here on

Every element in this book, from this chapter to the last one, is fetched with
`document.querySelector<...>('#someId')` and then checked against `null`.
There is no `as` anywhere from here on. It compiles, and it moves a problem you
could have fixed in the editor into your user's browser.
:::

## Text in, numbers out {#sec-types-for-elements-numbers}

An `<input>` gives you its content through `value`, and `value` is always a
string. Even an `<input type="number">` hands you a string, because the user
types characters and the browser passes on what they typed.

`Number(someString)` converts. `Number('7.5')` gives you the number `7.5`. Not
every string survives the trip, and `Number.isNaN(x)` answers whether `x` is
the special value you get back when the conversion failed. That check is what
stands between a user typing nonsense and your page showing `NaN` as a result.

::: {.research title="What comes back when the text is not a number?"}
The calculator you build next has to reject what the user types when it is not
a number, and it has to read which operation they picked from a `<select>`.
Both need details this book stops at.

1. `Number('abc')` and `Number('')` do not give you the same result. What does
   each one return?
2. What does `parseFloat('12abc')` return, and what does `Number('12abc')`
   return?
3. An `HTMLSelectElement` has a property that gives you the value of the option
   the user picked. What is it called, and where did you find it?

The exam is written without internet and without AI, so question 1 has to stick
in your head: the empty field is the case students get wrong every year.
:::

## Exercise: a calculator {#sec-types-for-elements-exercise}

{{< exercise calculator >}}

The page is ready: two text inputs with the ids `leftNumber` and `rightNumber`,
a `<select>` with the id `operator` holding the four options `+`, `-`, `*`, and
`/`, a button with the id `calculateButton`, an empty paragraph `result`, and
an empty paragraph `error` that the stylesheet paints red. The inputs are plain
text inputs on purpose, so that your check has something to catch.

You write `src/index.ts` from nothing. Delete what the starter put there.

1. Import the stylesheet as the first line: `import './styles.css';`. Run
   `npm start` and open the page. The labels sit in a column and the fields are
   in one narrow block, which tells you the CSS arrived.
2. Fetch all six elements with `document.querySelector<...>('#theId')`, each
   with the kind of element it is. The result and error paragraphs are
   `HTMLParagraphElement`.
3. Check for `null` and `throw` when an element is missing. One `if` with all
   six conditions joined by `||` is enough, and its message can name the page
   rather than a single id.
4. Add a `click` listener to the button. Inside it, read the two input values,
   convert them with `Number`, and read the chosen operator from the select
   element. Log all three with `console.log` and check in the browser console
   that a click gives you what you expect.
5. Refuse bad input. When a field is empty or holds something that is not a
   number, write a message such as `Please type a number into both fields.`
   into the error paragraph. Clear the result paragraph, then leave the
   function with `return`. Test an empty field and `12abc` before you go on,
   because they fail for different reasons.
6. Refuse division by zero. When the operator is `/` and the second number is
   `0`, write `You cannot divide by zero.` into the error paragraph, clear the
   result, and `return`.
7. Compute the result with a `switch` over the operator and show it in the
   result paragraph as a full line, for example `3.5 + 2 = 5.5`. Clear the
   error paragraph on the way, so a good calculation after a bad one leaves no
   red text behind.
8. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome reports.

Type `10 / 0`, then `3.5 + 2`. The red message must be gone when the result
appears. Try `12abc * 2` last, and watch the error come back.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

Add a fifth option to the `<select>` for the remainder operator `%`, and make
the calculator refuse a remainder by zero the same way it refuses a division by
zero.
:::
